## Introduction

Every Codespace you have opened arrived identical to every other one. A machine built from `codespace-starter` knows nothing about you. That is why GitHub Advanced ended with commands you run "once per machine," and why `connect-repo` exists.

This tutorial retires those commands. A **dotfile** is a configuration file whose name starts with a dot, which hides it from an ordinary `ls`. `.bashrc` configures the bash shell. `.gitconfig` configures Git.

###

The plan, in four parts:

1. Look at two settings a fresh Codespace lacks.
2. Build a private repo called `dotfiles` holding three small files, and push it.
3. Store two secrets, your GitHub token and your Census API key, where GitHub keeps secrets.
4. Turn dotfiles on, build a new Codespace, and check that everything arrived.

The repo you make is **permanent**. Every other repo in this course is scratch work. This one you keep. You will not open it as your workspace. Everything happens in the bash Terminal.

In the bash Terminal, run:

```bash

```

### Exercise 3

`~/.bashrc` runs every time you open a bash Terminal. In the bash Terminal, show the block about your prompt:

```bash
grep -A 2 short-prompt ~/.bashrc
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run grep -A 2 short-prompt ~/.bashrc. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ grep -A 2 short-prompt ~/.bashrc
# codespace-starter:short-prompt — short prompt for beginners (folder name + $).
PROMPT_COMMAND=''
PS1='\W \$ '
```

###

`PS1` holds your prompt, and `\W` means the name of the current directory. That is why the prompt changes as you `cd` around.

`codespace-starter` **appended** those lines to the end of `~/.bashrc` while the Codespace was being built. The file already belongs to somebody. In a few minutes you will add lines after theirs rather than replace it.

## Your Dotfiles Repo

Part two. You need a repo, and a way to get its files into your home directory.

### Exercise 1

In the bash Terminal, run `gh auth status`.

If it reports that you are **not** logged in, run the sign-in ritual from GitHub Advanced and then run `gh auth status` again:

```bash
unset GITHUB_TOKEN
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false
git config --global credential.helper store
printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\n' "$(gh auth token)" > ~/.git-credentials
```

The same command you used for `scratch-repo`, with `--private`. GitHub reads this repo with your own permissions, so private works as well as public, and there is no reason to publish your settings. Almost every dotfiles repo in the world is called `dotfiles`, so ours is too.

### Exercise 3

GitHub sets up your machine in one of two ways. If the repo has an **install script**, named `install.sh`, GitHub runs it and stops. If not, GitHub **symlinks** every dotted file in the repo into your home directory. We use a script, and the script appends small **fragments** to files that already exist.

Ask AI to create the first fragment, a file called `bashrc` in `/workspaces/dotfiles`, with exactly these two lines:

```bash
export COOLEST_TEACHER=Preceptor
alias agyd='agy --dangerously-skip-permissions'
```

In the bash Terminal, run `cat bashrc`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Ask AI to create a file called bashrc in /workspaces/dotfiles with exactly two lines: export COOLEST_TEACHER=Preceptor, and alias agyd='agy --dangerously-skip-permissions'. In the bash Terminal, run cat bashrc. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ cat bashrc
export COOLEST_TEACHER=Preceptor
alias agyd='agy --dangerously-skip-permissions'
```

###

No leading dot, on purpose. This is a fragment to append to `~/.bashrc`, not a file to install. If you ever deleted `install.sh`, GitHub would fall back to symlinking, and a file named `.bashrc` here would replace the real one.

### Exercise 4

Test the fragment before shipping it. In the bash Terminal, run these commands, one at a time:

```bash
source bashrc
echo $COOLEST_TEACHER
```

CP/CR.

```{r}

#| echo: false
learnr2::question(

  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ source bashrc
dotfiles $ echo $COOLEST_TEACHER
Preceptor
```

###

`source` runs a file's lines in the current shell, which is how `.bashrc` itself gets run. The effect reaches this one terminal only. A new terminal would still print nothing, because `~/.bashrc` has not changed.

### Exercise 5

Ask AI to create the second fragment, `gitconfig`, in `/workspaces/dotfiles`. Put your real name after `name =` and your GitHub username in the email address:

```ini
[user]
	name = Your Name
	email = YOUR-USERNAME@users.noreply.github.com
[init]
	defaultBranch = main
[alias]
	s = status --short --branch
	l = log --oneline --graph --decorate -20
[credential]
	helper =
	helper = !gh auth git-credential
```

In the bash Terminal, run `cat gitconfig`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Ask AI to create gitconfig in /workspaces/dotfiles with the contents shown, with your real name after name = and your GitHub username in the email address. In the bash Terminal, run cat gitconfig. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ cat gitconfig
[user]
	name = David Kane
	email = your-username@users.noreply.github.com
[init]
	defaultBranch = main
[alias]
	s = status --short --branch
	l = log --oneline --graph --decorate -20
[credential]
	helper =
	helper = !gh auth git-credential
```

###

`[user]` is what Git needs before it will commit. Outside a Codespace, a fresh machine does not know it. Use the `@users.noreply.github.com` address rather than your real one, because every commit carries its email into every public repo you push to.

### Exercise 6

Check that Git can read the fragment. In the bash Terminal, run:

```bash
git config --file gitconfig --list
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run git config --file gitconfig --list. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ git config --file gitconfig --list
user.name=David Kane
user.email=your-username@users.noreply.github.com
init.defaultbranch=main
alias.s=status --short --branch
alias.l=log --oneline --graph --decorate -20
credential.helper=
credential.helper=!gh auth git-credential
```

###

Git parsed every line, so the file is valid. The two `credential.helper` lines are deliberate. The empty one clears whatever helpers the machine came with. The second tells Git to ask `gh` for a password whenever it needs one.

### Exercise 7

Ask AI to create the third file, `install.sh`, in `/workspaces/dotfiles`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -e
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

printf '\n%s\n' "$(cat bashrc)" >> ~/.bashrc
printf '\n%s\n' "$(cat gitconfig)" >> ~/.gitconfig
```

In the bash Terminal, run `cat install.sh`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Ask AI to create install.sh in /workspaces/dotfiles with the contents shown. In the bash Terminal, run cat install.sh. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ cat install.sh
#!/bin/bash
set -e
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

printf '\n%s\n' "$(cat bashrc)" >> ~/.bashrc
printf '\n%s\n' "$(cat gitconfig)" >> ~/.gitconfig
```

###

`>>` **appends** to a file. A single `>` would overwrite it. Most dotfiles repos on the internet ship a whole `.bashrc`, which would wipe out the short prompt you looked at in the Introduction. **When you do not own a file, add to it rather than replace it.**

`$(cat bashrc)` is the text of the fragment. `printf` writes it with a newline before and after, so it can never glue itself onto the last line of the file, even when the fragment has no final newline. Files written by AI often lack one.

`set -e` stops the script at the first failure. `cd "$(dirname "$0")"` moves to wherever the script lives, since you do not know where GitHub will run it from.

### Exercise 8

In the bash Terminal, run `ls -l install.sh`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-10
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run ls -l install.sh. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ ls -l install.sh
-rw-rw-rw- 1 rstudio rstudio 137 Oct 23 14:22 install.sh
```

If yours already begins `-rwxrwxrwx`, the AI made the file executable for you. Carry on.

###

The ten characters at the left are the file's permissions. The first is `-` for a plain file. Then come three groups of three: what the owner may do, what the owner's group may do, and what everyone else may do. `r` is read, `w` is write, and `x` is execute. `-rw-rw-rw-` means anyone may read or write this file and nobody may run it.

### Exercise 9

GitHub runs the script only if it is executable. In the bash Terminal, run these commands, one at a time:

```bash
chmod +x install.sh
ls -l install.sh
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run chmod +x install.sh, then ls -l install.sh. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ chmod +x install.sh
dotfiles $ ls -l install.sh
-rwxrwxrwx 1 rstudio rstudio 137 Oct 23 14:22 install.sh
```

###

`chmod +x` sets the execute bit for everyone, and the `x` characters appear. A missing execute bit is the most common way a dotfiles repo silently does nothing. Git stores this bit, so it survives the trip to a new machine.

## What Does Not Belong In A Repo

Part three. Everything in `gitconfig` is a **setting**: true for years, and harmless if the whole world read it. Your GitHub token is a password. A password in a repo, even a private one, is a copy on GitHub, a copy on every machine you open, and a line in Git history forever. GitHub keeps a separate place for values like that.

<!-- TODO: images/secrets-one.png — the Codespaces secrets list showing GH_TOKEN with PPBDS/codespace-starter under repository access. -->

The list shows one secret, `GH_TOKEN`, with `PPBDS/codespace-starter` under its repository access.

`GH_TOKEN` is the name `gh` looks for, and `gh` prefers it to the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` that can only touch `codespace-starter`. ###

Two boxes on one page. **Dotfiles** deliver files you wrote: your name, your aliases, your prompt. Things you would not mind anyone reading. **Secrets** deliver values GitHub holds encrypted: your GitHub token, your Census key. Things you may one day need to revoke in a hurry. Part three is done.

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ tail -2 ~/.bashrc
export COOLEST_TEACHER=Preceptor
alias agyd='agy --dangerously-skip-permissions'
```

###

The last two lines of `.bashrc` are yours, and the starter's lines are still above them. That is `>>` at work, and it is why your prompt still reads `codespace-starter $`. More aliases, a `.gitignore_global`, R options: anything you would otherwise redo on every machine belongs in the same fragment.

R has your Census key and there is no `.Renviron` to hold it. The key came through the environment, from the secret, the same way `GH_TOKEN` reached `gh`. Every `get_acs()` call on this machine will work.

## Summary

You started with `echo $COOLEST_TEACHER` printing nothing. You finished with it printing `Preceptor` on a machine that did not exist when you began, and that machine was signed in to GitHub as you, knew your name, had `agyd`, and had your Census key.

###

You built a private repo called `dotfiles` holding `install.sh` and two fragments, `bashrc` and `gitconfig`, which the script **appends** to the real files. You put the two things that must not live in a repo, your GitHub token and your Census API key, in the Codespaces secrets `GH_TOKEN` and `CENSUS_API_KEY`. And you turned on the switch that delivers the repo to every Codespace you create.

###

From here on, a tutorial that says *create a repo called `whatever` and connect to it* needs no login step:

```bash
cd /workspaces
gh repo create whatever --public --clone
cd whatever
```

Then **File -> Open Folder...** on `/workspaces/whatever`. `connect-repo` still works. It checks whether you are signed in, finds that you are, and goes straight to creating the repo, dropping in `AGENTS.md` on the way.

###

One rule to carry forward: **settings that apply at creation do not reach a machine that already exists.** Dotfiles and secrets alike.
